summary: Describes the standardization cooperation between IEEE Project 802 and the IETF. It was developed jointly by authors from both groups and approved by the IEEE 802 Executive Committee. It replaces RFC 4441.

eli5.summary: Two groups build the pieces of networks. One makes the cables and wireless parts, the other makes the rules above them. This explains how the two groups work together.

questions: how do ieee 802 and the ietf work together
what is the difference between ieee 802 and ietf
subtitle: How two independent standards bodies, one for LANs and one for the Internet, coordinate their work.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802 and the IETF each build standards that depend on the other's, but they use different structures, vocabulary and decision rules, so conflicts and surprises are likely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how each organization works, then sets out how they exchange information about new work, review each other's drafts, use liaison managers and statements, and handle protocol parameter registries.
tldr.outcome: It changes no formal procedure of either body. It obsoletes RFC 4441 and is updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 7241 is an Informational RFC that obsoleted RFC 4441, and it is updated by RFC 9141.

sections.title: Why the Two Organizations Cooperate
sections.content:
This document sets out principles and guidelines for coordination between Project 802 of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE 802) and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). The objective is timely development of technical specifications that interoperate as much as possible with existing fixed and mobile Internet systems, devices and protocols.

Each organization keeps its own rules, including those for IPR policy, specification development, approval and maintenance. The RFC states that it does not change any formal practice or procedure of either one.

The motivation is dependency. Each body uses standards produced by the other, and some protocols even carry attributes that reflect the other's technology. The RFC notes that cooperation has a coordination cost, so the benefits must outweigh it. The IETF gains access to IEEE 802 expertise in the widely used LAN architecture, and IEEE 802 gains IETF expertise on IP datagram encapsulation, routing, transport, security and applications.
sections.eli5: Two builders each use the other's parts, so it helps if they talk. But each keeps running their own workshop their own way.

sections.title: How Each Organization Is Run
sections.content:
IEEE 802 is the LAN/MAN Standards Committee, a sponsor under the IEEE Standards Association. Its areas include Ethernet, bridging, wireless LAN, wireless PAN and wireless MAN. Work is done in Working Groups under an Executive Committee. Each Working Group has a chair and usually Task Groups, and Study Groups consider new projects and develop a Project Authorization Request (PAR). The Executive Committee and all Working Groups meet three times a year in plenary sessions, in March, July and November. Participants take part as individuals, must declare their affiliation, and gain voting membership through in-person attendance.

The IETF does its work in Working Groups, mostly on open public mailing lists. Working Groups are organized into areas, whose Area Directors together form the IESG. The IAB has oversight duties such as architectural oversight, standards process appeal and oversight of external liaisons. IETF participation is open to anyone, all participants act as individuals, and there is no IETF membership. Technical agreements are based on the consensus of Working Group participants, not negotiated with IETF leadership.
sections.eli5: One group has official members who must show up at meetings to vote. The other lets anyone join by email, and nobody is an official member.

sections.title: Structural and Cultural Differences
sections.content:
The two bodies use the same words for different things. Both have "Working Groups", but an IETF Area resembles an IEEE 802 Working Group, an IETF Working Group resembles an IEEE 802 Task Group, and an IETF BOF resembles an IEEE 802 Study Group. IETF directorates, which help Area Directors, have no IEEE 802 counterpart.

Decision-making differs most. The IETF uses rough consensus and its Working Groups do not vote; chairs may ask for a show of hands or take a hum, which is not a vote. IEEE 802 ultimately relies on a 75 percent vote to decide technical issues and 50 percent plus one for other issues. The IETF requires Working Group decisions to be made or confirmed on mailing lists, while most major IEEE 802 decisions are made in plenary or interim meetings, and meeting attendance is a condition of voting membership.

Other differences: IEEE 802 periodically reviews existing standards while the IETF has no formal periodic review, and the word "ballot" means different things. An IESG ballot signals that technical concerns have been addressed, and "no" is not one of its choices.
sections.eli5: One club makes decisions by voting at meetings. The other lets people talk online until nearly everyone agrees, and nobody calls that voting.

sections.title: Sharing Work Items and Reviewing Drafts
sections.content:
Each side is responsible for watching the other. IEEE 802 Working Groups review IETF charters and Internet-Drafts, and IETF Working Groups periodically review the IEEE 802 web site, where each plenary publishes status reports. An IEEE 802 project's charter is its approved PAR. A group proposing new work that may conflict with, overlap or depend on the other body's work must inform the other body's top-level coordination body, which decides whether cooperation is needed and notifies the affected groups. The RFC calls the shared New-Work mailing list a "belt and suspenders" backup.

Timing matters. IETF turnaround for new Working Group charters can be as short as two weeks. IEEE 802 PARs that introduce new functionality must be available for review no less than 30 days before the Monday of the plenary where they are considered, and comments on PARs are due by 5:00 PM Tuesday of that plenary.

For review, IEEE 802 drafts go through Task Group review, Working Group ballot and Sponsor ballot. Initial ballots last at least 30 days and recirculation ballots at least 10 days, and non-voters can still submit comments that must be considered. The IETF has no ballots to decide consensus, and useful input points are Working Group adoption, Working Group Last Call and IETF Last Call. Formal communication between the bodies goes through liaison managers and liaison statements; a liaison manager does not speak for the appointing organization but helps ensure neither side is surprised.
sections.eli5: Each club watches the other's announcements and agrees to warn the other early about new projects. Both also let outsiders comment on drafts before they are finished.

sections.title: Protocol Parameter Registries
sections.content:
Both organizations keep registries of assigned values. The IETF uses IANA as a central authority, with allocation policies that vary by registry, from first come first served to "Standards Action" (an approved Standards Track RFC) and "Expert Review". IEEE uses the IEEE Registration Authority, overseen by the IEEE Registration Authority Committee (RAC), and each IEEE 802 Working Group also keeps its own identifier registry, for items such as Object Identifiers and OpCodes.

Ethertypes are scarce. The IEEE RAC will not assign a new Ethertype to a new IETF protocol until the IESG has approved the specification for publication as an RFC, though "early allocation" is possible in exceptional cases when the IESG requests it. "Playpen" Ethertypes exist for development and experimentation. Because some registries are joint-use, each side must check the other's registry references during review: IEEE 802 documents before Sponsor ballot, and IETF documents during IANA review in IETF Last Call.
sections.eli5: Both groups keep lists of numbers and names that are already taken. Before using a number from the other group's list, you check it is really yours.

sections.title: Examples of Cooperation
sections.content:
Appendix A gives three examples. For MIB review, MIB modules for IEEE 802.1 and 802.3 used to be developed in IETF working groups, but because of travel budgets the work moved to IEEE 802 with IETF expert review, as documented in RFC 4663. An IEEE 802 group can ask the IETF Operations and Management Area Director for a "MIB Doctor".

For AAA review, IEEE 802 groups needing new AAA applications should send a liaison request to the IETF. Attributes of general utility should be allocated from the IETF standard attribute space instead of creating IEEE 802 Vendor-Specific Attributes. For EAP review, groups adding support for the Extensible Authentication Protocol should request a security review, and the appendix notes that the EAP WG reviewed IEEE 802.16 at its request.

The Security Considerations section says the document describes cooperation procedures and has no direct Internet security implications.
sections.eli5: When one club needs expert help from the other, such as checking a design for security, it just sends a request and the other club's experts take a look.
